speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the oral notice given by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) last Thursday at the close of the sitting, and as published in Votes and Proceedings for Friday, I move:
That on Monday, April 28. 1952, and every Monday thereafter to the end of the session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all business except the introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.
I would hope, however, that it might be understood that there would be allotted today as much time to private members' business as was taken last Monday to deal with the motion to set up the committee on the readjustment of representation.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there were any reason before us why the motion should be adopted at this time, I would be prepared to support it, as I think many other members would. On other occasions in the past similar motions have received assent from members at a time when it was clearly demonstrated that urgent matters required consideration. But no urgency-and I submit this to hon. members-has been demonstrated, and no such case has been presented to us. On the contrary there are many reasons why the rights of private members should be preserved, in this as in other sessions.
This session has followed a pattern which surely calls for the attention of all members. Tomorrow we will be into the third calendar month of the session. Outside of the strictly formal bills which were called for following the approval of the supplementary estimates,
the only measure placed before the house for consideration by way of legislation is a bill that was introduced at the very outset to deal with an emergent situation which had arisen because of the outbreak of the foot-and-mouth disease.
It is not necessary to say that there was an extended debate on the speech from the throne, or that there has been already a debate for some days on the budget. Those debates of necessity were more extended, and doubtless the discussion was more discursive, because no direction has been given to the business of this house since the session began on February 28. There has been no pattern, there has been no lead, there has been no indication to hon. members of the things they would really be called upon to discuss except for those private measures, either by way of bill or by way of motion, brought forward by private members.
It is true that we had a discussion on external affairs and national defence. It is true that after repeated requests the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated the concurrence of the government in the suggestion that had been made that there should be separate debates on external affairs and national defence. But the effectiveness of those debates was to a great extent stultified by the fact that, for whatever reasons may have been put forward, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) saw fit to address a club in New York just a few days before that debate when every subject that could be brought forward was brought forward there. Then a few days later he went on the radio over a national network and devoted his attention largely to one party in this house in a manner which introduced a spirited debate on what the motives of that party really were.

I have referred to the fact that without explanation or justification of any kind we are proceeding at this time with the budget debate in the absence of the Minister of Finance. That very fact is an affront not only to members of this house but to all Canadians at a time when we are considering a budget that will be the basis of the enormous taxation to be imposed in Canada this year. It is directly relevant to the motion before us.
There can be only one suggested argument in support of such a debate proceeding in the absence of the Minister of Finance. That would be that no matter what argument is put forward, the ears of the government will be deaf in any event. If we have reached

that point, then it would be wise for the government to go one step farther and end the farce by introducing a motion that all debate should come to an end, and let any member who has anything to put forward simply file a written argument and have it appear in the record, because the government does not intend to listen to it in any event.
The reason for the arguments that are put forward is that the government may hear these arguments. We are now dealing with a pattern which has been established, namely, that ministers primarily concerned first make their arguments outside of the house. Then when these matters come up in the house they give scant attention to the members, and, having presented their case do not even bother to listen to the arguments that are put forward. Do not let any hon. member say that the arguments that have been put forward have not been arguments worth listening to. Speeches have been made in the house that should have been listened to by every member of the house and many more members of the government than have ever been here at any time since the budget debate started. Speeches of vital importance have been presented.
There have been speeches made with respect to the deplorable situation in the farming industry, including dairying, and the textile and other industries across the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Yet on many occasions not more than two ministers of the crown have even thought it worth while to listen to these arguments, even though the responsible minister, the Minister of Finance, is not here and apparently has no immediate intention of returning, so far as one can see at the moment.

-and why it would be wholly unnecessary to adopt this motion if the government really wanted to get ahead with the business. If the government does want to get ahead with its business, then let it introduce the bills it has under consideration. It is not reasonable to believe that at this stage of the session the government has not ready all the legislation it intends to introduce. Let it bring forward that legislation and move it into committee so it can be given consideration, instead of holding it back until the end of the session when there will not be adequate opportunity to examine it, as has happened so often in the past.
I iam raising these points because we have urged over and over again that the rules of the house do make it possible to deal with the bills and resolutions of private members as well as the regular business of the house, as long as the members have some idea when that business is going to be dealt with. Let no one make the suggestion by way of reply that the government has sought to expedite proceedings and that

long debates have taken place on every motion it has introduced. There have been debates, but those debates have taken place because hon. members have no way of knowing whether or not they are going to have an opportunity of raising the questions they want to raise. They do not know whether this session the government is going to change its habits and let debate follow an orderly pattern, or whether it is going to follow the practice of the last several sessions and leave the important things until the last, when the heat of the summer and the desire to get home will make it very difficult to discuss adequately the measures brought before the house.
This motion will have the effect of further limiting the rights of private members, which already have been limited greatly. During the years of war and immediately after, the habit grew of setting aside the rules; but surely now we have reached a time when we can abide by the rules. If those rules need amendment, let the amendments be introduced in the ordinary way. Instead of motions to suspend rules, let us have motions to change the rules if in fact isuch changes should be made. But at a time when we have so little before us, at a time when the Minister of Finance does not think the budget debate is sufficiently important to be here for it, let us not adopt a motion of this kind which deprives private members of the opportunity to have real debates on subjects that are of real concern to the people of Canada.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
On
various occasions when motions of this kind have been presented to the house I have protested on behalf of the private members who are associated with me. To a very large extent I agree with what has been said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in regard to the necessity of members of this house safeguarding in every particular the rights of private members. I am not suggesting for one moment that the government with its large majority wishes to exercise some kind of dictatorship over all of us to override the House of Commons, but I do support what was said by the leader of the opposition in his concluding remarks. Bit by bit the rights of private members have been restricted, largely because of the necessities of war. Prior to the war private members' days were looked upon as being embedded in the rules of the house and were not interfered with without very good reason; and always, may I say, after there had been some discussion and consultation with the whips or leaders of the opposition parties.
Business of the House
Having watched the loss of the rights of private members in this house over a period of years-and rights have been lost-it is good that once in a while private members should assert themselves and demand that their rights be retained in every particular. Under wartime conditions private members were willing at all times to forgo many of their rights. I remember one or two regular sessions when there were no private members' days at all. That was because of the emergencies then existing, and was by agreement.
I believe those of us who from time to time criticize the conduct of the business of the house should take some responsibility for endeavouring to provide the better organization of that business. There is no question but that the manner in which we conduct the business of this parliament does not reflect much credit upon the House of Commons. The rules which have been provided very largely for the protection of those of us who are private members from time to time need to be reconsidered and revised.
I agree with the criticism of the leader of the opposition in regard to statements made outside this house and the absence of ministers when such important matters as the budget are under consideration. I think that does show a lack of regard for this parliament.
Coming now to the private members' resolutions, a number of those resolutions on the order paper are of very great importance, not so much to the private members themselves as to their constituents and to members of all parties from one end of this country to the other. These resolutions can only be moved in the form in which they are brought before the house, namely "that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given."
I have felt that from time to time the government has paid no attention to the expressed will of this parliament.
I am not going to discuss the income tax exemption for medical expenses, the milk subsidy, and so on, but resolutions concerning these matters were approved by this house, in one case unanimously, for the consideration of the government. I do say this: The only opportunity, other than by moving an amendment to the budget or the motion for an address in reply to the speech of His Excellency at the opening of the session-the only opportunity a private member has to bring before this house matters of importance not only to their constituents but to the whole of Canada, is by the filing of private members' resolutions. They do perform a useful function in this parliament. Consequently I do not like to see any attempt made to restrict the

Business of the House
rights of private members. If this privilege is to be circumscribed in any way, or dispensed with for the moment, it should be done by agreement rather than by the adoption of a motion.
I am quite sure the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would find that most hon. members would be willing to accede to the request of the government, if the government were in a position of some difficulty regarding the business of the house. As has been said this afternoon, we do not know as yet what legislation is coming before us, and we are therefore in an extremely difficult position in attempting to make a judgment. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I think the organization of the business of this house must be reconsidered. I suggest that private members' days be continued until at least we have complete knowledge of the legislation that is coming before us, and until we are sure that the committees of the house are going to be at work. I am extremely anxious that the committee on agriculture should go into the matter of the foot-and-mouth disease. I cannot see any reason why the government has delayed consideration of that matter. I am sure that all members are willing to cooperate to facilitate the business of the house, provided that we know what the business of the house is, and can form a mature judgment as to the need for forgoing some rights of private members.

I should like to take a moment to say that we are anxious to do what we can to help the government get its program before the house and have the business completed. But at the same time we do feel we should not take any action, except after careful consideration and by agreement, that would further abridge the rights of private members. For this reason I find myself very largely in agreement with the other two party leaders on this side of the floor.
I would suggest that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) give careful consideration to frequent conferences between the party whips to see if it would not be possible to organize the business of the house in such a manner as to speed things along. If we were given some idea of what is coming up, we could be prepared when that item of business came before the house and would thus facilitate the dispatch of business. On this matter I must stand with the other party leaders.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words with reference to a matter which has a bearing on the motion that is now

before us. On Tuesday, April 1, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) moved a motion to take away Wednesdays as private members' days, a request was made by the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) to which the Prime Minister made a conditional reply. I feel that the substance of that reply should even yet be implemented.
It is for that reason I rise to ask the Prime Minister to give further consideration to what was asked for on that occasion.
As the Prime Minister and the house will remember, Monday, March 31, was to have been a private members' day. By unanimous consent we gave it up as a private members' day so that the government might have it for the consideration of supplementary estimates. Accordingly the next day, when the Prime Minister moved that Wednesdays be taken away, the member for Rosetown-Biggar requested that the loss of the day before might be made up in some way. In his reply the Prime Minister indicated that there were certain difficulties, but he did say this, as recorded at page 999 of Hansard for April 1, 1952:
Perhaps we might consider suspending this order a week from Wednesday, or try to make it up in some other way that would satisfy hon. members.
I would point out that the Wednesday referred to was Wednesday, April 9, but the order was not suspended on that day. Instead, we considered the Japanese peace treaty, which was government business. Thus, so far as the private members are concerned there has been no compensation as yet for the loss of that full Monday, March 31. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that whatever may be the disposition of the motion now before us, which is designed to take away Mondays as private members' days, the Prime Minister should still consider the point which he said he would consider on April 1, and arrange with the various groups in the house for the provision of at least one more Wednesday for private members' motions.

It was merely reminiscent of many such performances and outbursts before the election of 1949. In thinking it over I recalled a number of occasions when it was the privilege of the hon. gentleman to lecture the members of this house on the way in which the proceedings of this house should, in his opinion, be

carried on, instead of being carried on as they have been in the long and somewhat fruitful years of the life of this house when the hon. gentleman was not a member of it.
It has been suggested that there should be frequent conferences between the whips of the groups. I think that is a very good suggestion, but it would be necessary for the whips of the groups to report to the leaders of the groups they represent that there had been such conferences so that those leaders of the groups might not be taking attitudes differing from the understandings that seemed to have been reached between the whips.

Mr. Speaker, the house may be interested to learn at this time that General Matthew Ridgway, United States army, was today appointed by the North Atlantic council to succeed General Dwight D. Eisenhower as supreme allied commander for Europe. This announcement was made this afternoon in Paris by Lord Ismay who had presided over the first meeting of the reorganized council as vice-chairman. At that first meeting this morning the President of the United States was requested to put forward the name of an American to succeed General Eisenhower. He put forward General Ridg-way's name, and General Ridgway was appointed by the council this afternoon.
The general feeling which has been held towards General Eisenhower for his services to NATO was, I think, very well expressed by Lord Ismay this morning when he said:
Our hearts are filled with pride and gratitude for what General Eisenhower has done since he was appointed supreme commander in Europe. It may well be that when history comes to be written the contributions which he has made towards saving peace will be acclaimed as no less worthy of renown than his contributions towards winning the second world war.
IMr. Speaker.]
General Ridgway's distinguished military career and, in particular, his recent post of commander of United Nations forces in Korea, show him to be well qualified for the important duties of supreme commander of the forces of North Atlantic countries in Europe. It is also gratifying to learn that President Truman has expressed his agreement that General Gruenther should remain as chief of staff to the new supreme commander, a post where he has been so successful and effective under General Eisenhower.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a supplementary answer to a question of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) which was drst answered on March 12, 1952, as found at page 352 of Hansard. The question is as follows:
1.	Did the various provincial governments undertake a survey to find out, among other things, the number of physically incapacitated persons in Canada?
2.	If so, has the survey been completed?
3.	What are the particulars disclosed regarding the number, age, and financial standing of those disabled persons?
4.	Will a pension scheme be introduced at the present session to relieve the distress of those persons?
The answer is as follows:
1,	2 and 3. See reply tabled on March 12, 1952, Hansard, page 352.
4. The experience of foreign countries suggests that disability pensions should be closely associated with rehabilitation services which are designed to restore the disabled person to productive employment. Without remedial health, vocational guidance and training services, the cost of disability pensions may run unnecessarily high, without achieving this goal. On February 20, 21, and 22 the national advisory committee on rehabilitation of disabled persons set up as a result of last year's conference
in Toronto, held its first meeting. It will review all aspects of the needs of disabled persons, and make recommendations from time to time.
Our new old age assistance and old age security programs will between them provide pensions for an estimated 45,000 totally and permanently handicapped persons. Allowances for blind persons will provide financial aid for approximately 8,500 more this year. Approximately 160,000 disabled veterans are receiving pensions and an additional number are being looked after under war veterans allowances.
Through the national health grants program substantial assistance is available to the disabled as follows:
(a)	The government has provided for a sum of more than $4 million for a tuberculosis control grant part of which is available for "the provision of free treatment including rehabilitation".
(b)	There is provision for a crippled children's grant of over $500,000 "to assist the provinces in an intensive program for the prevention and correction of crippling conditions in children, rehabilitation and training".
(c)	Under the general public health grant very substantial sums are available to extend diagnostic and treatment services for those afflicted by arthritis and rheumatism or polio.
(d)	The government has provided for a sum of more than $5 million, part of which is available for the rehabilitation of backward children and of mentally ill patients, under the mental health grant.
The provinces, under well-established workmen's compensation plans, provide pensions for the victims of industrial accidents. Approximately one-third of the cases in receipt of mothers' allowances are the result of disabilities which impair earnings. Some provinces offer special allowances for persons

suffering from tuberculosis, and Newfoundland and Ontario have in recent years provided incapacitation allowances.
The province of Ontario has at its 1952 session just passed legislation providing for disability pensions. There is no indication at the present time that other provinces intend to follow this example.
It is the intention of the federal government to work in close co-operation with the provinces and interested organizations in a constructive approach to the complex problems involved in the various types of disabilities which impair the ability of individuals to work.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed that the report to which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar refers as having been made by "F" division, C.I.B., Regina town station, R.C.M.P., dated March 20, 1952, with respect to the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, is a report made to his superior officers by a constable of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police acting as an investigator in this matter. The Department of Justice and the government have consistently taken the position that reports made to their superior officers by members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police concerning investigations which they have been instructed to conduct have always been withheld from production in the House of Commons upon the ground that it is not in the public interest to produce them.
The reasons for the taking of this position will be obvious to anyone who gives the matter thought. Not only are the police investigators instructed to ascertain all the relevant facts, but they are encouraged to submit to their superior officers their own theories and their own hypotheses as to what interpretations might be drawn from these facts in further investigation into the matter. They are encouraged to suggest further lines of inquiry. They are encouraged, and indeed instructed, in the case of an investigation into a crime, to suggest in strictest confidence all those whom they regard as possible suspects, however slight may be their own reasons for suspecting these other persons, in order that their superior officers to whom these confidential reports are made may, by considering these confidential reports along with other confidential reports received from other investigating officers, draw conclusions as to what further investigations may be necessary, or even ultimate conclusions as to guilt and the identity of the guilty party or parties.
If the investigating officer does not know at the time he makes his report that it will be privileged from publication he, I suggest, will be hesitant about suggesting hypotheses, particularly in scientific and other fields in which, if he is not qualified as an expert witness, his oral evidence would not even be received. He will be most hesitant about naming suspects if he knows that the names of such suspects are to be published and their reputations prejudiced or ruined when in fact

they may be completely guiltless. Therefore the production of these confidential reports would destroy much of their value. For these reasons the Department of Justice and the government feel that in the present instance we must follow our uniform and invariable practice of refusing to table the confidential report referred to in the hon. member's motion. Without arguing the matter unless it becomes necessary, I would submit the following citations: 1943, Hansard, volume 1, page 202; 1943, Hansard, volume 4, page 4193; 1945, Hansard, volume 2, page 1929.

CO-OPERATION AMONG SPONSOR NATIONS OP NATO
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, if an invitation is received by the parliament of Canada to appoint delegates to meet with delegates from the legislatures of the sponsor nations of NATO, with a view to discussing their closer co-operation within the framework of the United Nations Organization, the government should give consideration to the acceptance of the invitation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, obviously the motion in my name which you have just read will not be as controversial as some of the other matters which have come up for discussion today, and that perhaps is fortunate. I hope that there will be support for this motion from members of the various parties throughout the house. As a motion it is not entirely satisfactory to myself because it is a compromise designed to get as much support as possible and, also, of course, a motion to ensure a debate in the house on NATO and the necessity for making it into an adequate and effective instrument for our purposes.
I am asking that, if an invitation is extended to the parliament of Canada to send delegates to meet with members from the legislatures of the sponsor nations of NATO, we accept it. The question arises: Who is going to bell the cat, who is going to issue this invitation? Speaking for myself, I should like to see Canada issue the invitation. I can see no reason indeed why we should not take such a lead for we have nothing to lose but our own fears. On the other hand we have everything to gain.
The more I consider the international situation and the way in which in certain aspects it is deteriorating the more convinced I become that members of parliament throughout the western democracies and all citizens will be terribly negligent in their responsibilities if they do not explore every avenue which can lead to a greater security for our people. It is possible that such a conference as I have in mind might be a failure, although I do not think it would be. I am prepared to take that chance. Some may argue that if it is a failure it will set back the cause which we have supported for an indeterminate number of years. I doubt it. What I am concerned about is finding out whether or not those ideas which many of us hold, ideas designed to make NATO stronger, have validity. The only way we can do that is by holding such a conference.
I am a believer in Atlantic union as the best way of strengthening the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I wish to make it abundantly clear that as a supporter of Atlantic union I am in no way in the slightest opposed or hostile to the United Nations or to what the United Nations is trying to do. What I am trying to do is to make the United Nations stronger by trying to make NATO stronger.
I have no intention of going over the basic arguments for union which I adduced last year in the house. The sponsor nations which I have in mind, apart from ourselves, are the United Kingdom, the United States,

United Nations
France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. What I would like to see, and here I speak personally, is a union among those countries, so that we might have a common foreign policy, a common defence policy, a common currency, a common citizenship and of course a common policy along lines of trade.
Some will say today that that is visionary. It may well be. Others will say that it is revolutionary, but that it certainly is not for what we are doing is proceeding along the lines of the precedents which we have established in the past. What strikes me most forcibly is that if war comes and we are to wage it successfully and efficiently that sort of union must come about for our own preservation. Therefore it would be so much better were we to try to achieve it, to lay the foundation for it now when we are at peace even if it is a somewhat uncertain and unsettled peace.
Those who believe in union of the North Atlantic democracies have in mind a triple goal, a threefold objective. We wish to achieve freedom, security and prosperity for our peoples. It is lamentable to think that within seven years of the conclusion of a war which shook the world we are spending more than 50 per cent of our national budget on defence. We are not spending it willingly, we are doing it because we are compelled to by extraneous forces but we have to do it. We are going to spend this year on defence five times the amount of the entire budget of Canada twenty years ago and yet we are no nearer peace today than we were in 1945. Perhaps we are a little nearer than we were in 1948, but that is the best that can be said.
That being so, it is time to re-examine and re-assess the security system which we have had in the past and to some extent to which we still cling. I maintain that the needs of today demand that that security system be rebuilt. This does not mean that we scrap the instruments which we have at hand, but rather that we use them in a way which will give us the security which we crave. The only chance of safety for the nations of this world, perhaps the only possibility for many people to live in this world, is to make war impossible. The question is: How do we go about it?
One of the best ways of going about it is to make the Atlantic community a reality. The Atlantic community has come far within the last few years but still we are talking rather than doing. I have inveighed frequently in the past against the policy of the western powers as being almost entirely a

negative policy, a policy designed to stop communism rather than a positive policy designed to promote the concept of democracy and freedom throughout the world. We are not going to inflame the minds of men by kindling enthusiasm for something which is entirely negative, but on the other hand if we make our policies positive, if we make policies for something instead of against something, then we shall get the support of peoples who are still unhappily somewhat hesitant.
I believe that under Atlantic union the freedom of all the individuals who were members of it would be enhanced. After all, the stress in a union such as I envisage is on the individual citizen and not upon the national governments. It is the individual citizen who is all-important. My suggestion is that we ask the citizen to transfer some of his personal sovereignty to a still greater international organization. Those of us who have only a smattering of history remember what happened in the United States before union was formed and in Canada before the dominion was formed. At that time the citizens were asked to transfer their sovereignty beyond the state and the province, to the union as it was in the United States and to the Dominion of Canada as it was here. I am suggesting that we have to extend and transfer that sovereignty even further today if we are going to be safe in the years to come. By so widening our individual sovereignty we shall automatically increase our individual security.
I have enumerated the seven nations with which I should like to enter into such an agreement. I mention them because we have a common heritage of culture, we are steeped in the same concepts of democracy. We cherish the liberties which we have in common and we have the same devotion to freedom. Above all, in such a union I am convinced that the rights of the minorities throughout these countries would be protected even more adequately than is the case just now. Today the rights of minorities are protected sometimes by a written constitution, sometimes by an unwritten constitution. Under union not only would the national constitution be operative to protect minorities, there would be legislation based upon the union which would give still greater protection.
I submit that this policy of co-operation among these nations will give still greater security in the world. If we have greater security it follows that we shall thereby enlarge our freedom. That security which we desire is growing, slowly it is true, and we welcome that growth.

The situation which exists in NATO today is indeed a far cry from that which existed a year ago when I spoke in a similar debate. I said then that the machinery whereby the supreme commander could get directives was slow and cumbersome and, indeed, dangerous in the sense -that it might lull us into a false sense of security. Now the machinery is being streamlined, and we welcome it. General Ridgway will have the opportunity, denied to his predecessor for obvious reasons, of getting decisions much more quickly by the council.
Yet the faot remains that in NATO we are still putting the cart before the horse. We are still insistent on building up a military machine without as yet creating the civilian control which is so desirable. I cannot think offhand of another example in history where that has been done. Usually nations have collaborated and co-operated on a political basis first, and from that co-operation the military machine has come. Such, for understandable reasons, has not been the situation with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It was essential that we build up our defences as rapidly as possible. We are doing that; we are achieving the defences which we need.
The next step to be taken, and the most important one, is that we create some form of democratic control of the armed forces that are being built up in Europe. It causes one to think seriously when we realize that within two or three years General Ridgway may have under him in Europe as many as a million men and under my concept of what is an appropriate state of combat readiness, ready to defend immediately against any attack. A force of a million men is an extraordinary force to control, and in my opinion the only way it could be done adequately would be through some form of Atlantic union. But if we cannot achieve that just now-and I am afraid that we cannot

there is an alternative by which we can create some form of accountability. That is by forming a North Atlantic assembly. I shall mention that later at greater length.
What is important, and what I am sure the ministers who have attended North Atlantic Treaty Organization meetings realize as fully as anybody else, is that we cannot have security by military means alone but that we have to have economic co-operation and support in a far greater way than has been the case in the past. In other words, we have to make article 2 of NATO work. It is in our interests in Canada to make Europe prosperous. The more prosperous Europeans are the greater is the market for those things which we produce and sell. But unhappily, with certain exceptions, on this continent our history has been for the last
United Nations
six years that, while we were willing to help Europe with arms, we were equally willing to hinder Europe with tariffs. We are prepared to give with the one hand and to take away with the other.
I of course believe that with the creation of a free trade area among these nations we should achieve a prosperity unparalleled in history and even yet undreamed of. It may be that in so far as the general reduction of tariffs is concerned the United States is the principal culprit, but at the moment it is not my intention to allot blame. Rather I wish to further my thesis. Whether the United States became industrially the most powerful nation in the world through tariffs is questionable. I do not think so. Nor do I think the United' States1 became such a powerful nation entirely owing to the ability and drive of its people. The real reason for the United States being so strong today is that the industrialists of that country had a tremendous area in which to sell their wares. They had a great population for whom they could manufacture and sell on a mass production basis. So the people of the United States, because of the great area in which they live and their great population, are able to get cheap production and mass production as a result of the size of the market, and accordingly their standard of living is high.
But what would happen if a market of that size were doubled within a short time? If I were an American my instinctive reaction would be that one effect of a free trade area in this group would be that there would be no more economic aid required for Europe, and that as a United States citizen I would not have to tax myself to provide this assistance to my allies. The credit needs of Europe could then be satisfied by public as well as by private investment. In Europe we should find that capital would no longer be frozen by controls necessitated of course by the chronic shortage of dollars, while the Americans and we in Canada might conceivably be willing to risk our capital in Europe because of the lack of controls. I am certain that were this free trade area to emerge there would be millions, and indeed tens of millions, of dollars available for investment on both sides of the Atlantic. There would be great prosperity.
Coming as I do from western Canada, I can see the great advantages which would accrue to that part of the country if the European nations who are our allies today had the dollars they require to buy the raw products we produce. I can see the great advantage which would accrue to farmers, fishermen, fruit growers, lumber producers, and indeed to all our raw material producers. It would be in our economic interest to do that, but

United Nations
the majority have not yet realized just where our economic interest lies. This aspiration will undoubtedly be classified as visionary, no matter how essential it is to our common welfare.
The all-important fact is that the situation in Europe today is probably as precarious as it has been since the war ended. The nations of Europe who are our allies are steadily losing their markets in Asia. The market in China is lost. The market in Indonesia has been partially lost. War has disrupted Indochina. The pattern of trade in India and Pakistan is not yet clear. Australia has decided to cut its imports by some 50 per cent, and the nations that are going to be most severely hurt and most badly affected are the nations in Europe. Where then are they going to find markets for their exports? The only area I can think of that is readily available is on the North American continent, and there is no sign yet that we are willing to take European goods. There is no sign yet that we are agreeable to implementing to the fullest article 2 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Therefore we are left with the very simple fact that we shall be compelled, if we want to keep our allies strong, to pour out economic aid to Europe. If we continue to do so we are justified in asking- to what sort of allies? They will be allies, they will be governments, they will be nations which will be very much under the gun. They will be governments under pressure of events at home, and the most serious pressure of all will be that of a falling and constantly reduced standard of living with its inevitable concomitant that the lower standard of living will give encouragement to the communist parties within those countries. By our default the men of Moscow may win.
After all, with the standards of living of their people falling, and with no market in which they can sell their goods, the governments of these countries will be compelled to cut their expenditures on defence, and that is the simple fact of the situation. Therefore by default we in North America will have weakened our allies, and of course disastrously weakened ourselves. The picture I draw is pessimistic, and yet I believe it is an accurate blueprint of the future. What we have not yet realized is that the Achilles heel of the west is the tariff structure of the western nations. Some may say: Why do the Europeans not enter into a union of their own? The answer is that a European union would solve none of the problems of Europe.
European union would not solve the perpetual dollar imbalance which perplexes Europe today. European union would not

give our European allies more dollars. European union would not give Europe the security it wants, because Europe cannot be secure without the assistance of North America, and we in North America must realize that we can have no security without the assistance of Europe. The other day I had the opportunity of chatting with the foreign minister of one of the NATO countries, who happened to be in Ottawa. He was quite outspoken and told me that in his opinion the only salvation of Europe lay not in European union but in Atlantic union, and that his country had gone so far as to amend its constitution to make entry into such a federation a possibility.
Here I repeat words which I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will remember: if the North Atlantic community is to endure it must rest on something broader and deeper than military co-operation alone. In other words we come back to article 2 of the treaty. There are some in the various countries belonging to NATO who regard article 2 somewhat in the form of holy water to be sprinkled upon an instrument of power politics. That is a cynical outlook; it is a defeatist attitude, which may yet cost us dear. If any holding these views should be appointed to any national delegation to Paris we might find them not at all prepared to carry out to the uttermost the policies of their home governments, and this is something which must be guarded against. Those officials who go to Paris to attend NATO must be men who are convinced that arising from defence needs will come collaboration in other fields. We have gone a long way in military co-operation. We will need to go just as far and even further in economic co-operation, and it is essential that all the officials sent to Paris should be, so far as is humanly possible, men who are convinced that article 2 can be the reality for which we hope.
In my own mind I am convinced that the surest way to make article 2 a reality is through Atlantic union; but in the absence of such a union I am content to advocate the creation of a North American assembly. Great benefit may be derived from parliamentarians in various countries meeting each other, discussing their problems and becoming more and more conscious of mutual needs. Unquestionably there will be clashes of opinion and conflicts of ideas, which we should welcome; but I am convinced that if such an assembly were attended by men of good will and integrity, great good could come out of it.
Let us admit also that we are making progress in NATO in ways other than defence.

Once we get rid of the froth and spume of what happened at Lisbon we can see that certain real achievements have been made. For instance, two or three years ago it would have been fantastic to suppose that three individual men, not representatives of governments, would be asked and even encouraged to examine national budgets and advise sovereign nations as to how they should order their finances for the common good. That is really extraordinary; yet what is extraordinary today will be commonplace tomorrow.
Equally interesting is the fact that the decisions of the NATO council are being accepted by the member governments, by and large. I say "by and large" because owing to its constitutional structure the United States does not find itself in the same position as, let us say, the United Kingdom or Canada. In our case the Secretary of State for External Affairs, with the approval of the government, can embark upon or support a certain policy in the NATO council knowing he will be supported when he comes back to parliament. The Secretary of State of the United States can also support a policy in the NATO council, but he has no guarantee that he will have the approval of congress or the senate when he returns to Washington. Nevertheless, even admitting that, governments today are accepting the decisions of the council. As time goes on and NATO develops, more and more its decisions will be accepted by national governments.
That being so, what is NATO today, apart from being an alliance of some fourteen nations? NATO is a loosely knit assembly of diplomats, senior civil servants, admirals, generals, air marshals and all the necessary and requisite camp followers. Only occasionally do ministers who are elected representatives sit in on the councils of NATO, though undoubtedly they will have the last word. But as long as that is the case; as long as the elected representatives of the people are divorced from what NATO is actually doing, so long will there be no real sense of community developed. I am convinced that one of the urgent requirements of the day is that elected representatives of the people should help more directly in framing the policy of NATO.
That brings me back to the concept of the North Atlantic assembly. In a couple of days we are going to have the privilege of a visit from a distinguished United States delegation, which is coming to Ottawa to discuss with Canadian parliamentarians the possibility of setting up a North Atlantic assembly. Its members will include Senator Gillette of Iowa, Senator Sparkman of Alabama, Congressman Leroy Johnson of
United Nations
California and the Hon. Owen Roberts, formerly a justice of the United States supreme court. I have no idea what conclusions will be arrived at as a result of these meetings, but we can be certain they will be stimulating and I hope the first of many of a like nature. We shall be discussing the possibility of creating a North Atlantic assembly. Again I have no idea what shape such an assembly would take. Possibly it might be along the lines of the assembly of Europe, with the council of NATO acting as a sort of interim cabinet until we can get something much closer to the European idea.

I do not hold that view. I think that in such an assembly there would be quite sufficient to discuss without getting into classified matters. The most important thing to be discussed, of course, would be the broad outlines and objectives of policy of the North Atlantic organization. If I were to put my aims and hopes into four short, succinct sentences I could do no better than quote these four points coming from a group of people in the United Kingdom who believe much as I do. They are:
1.	To secure peace we need a global defence policy for the western and Atlantic community acting in partnership.
2.	To carry out a common defence policy we need a common foreign policy.
3.	To maintain and improve the standard and quality of living we need a partnership in economic policy.
4.	To achieve this partnership in defence, foreign and economic affairs, we need regular meetings of a council of ministers, served by a common secretariat and guided by a common assembly.
When we arrive at that partnership, Mr. Speaker, when we arrive at that assembly, then the bones of NATO will become clothed in flesh and blood; then, indeed, the North Atlantic community of which we have heard so much will have become a reality.

I feel, Mr. Speaker, that possibly I ought to say a word or two on this resolution, although its terms are not, as I understand them, such as to require any statement of policy on behalf of the government. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, if an invitation is received by the parliament of Canada to appoint delegates to meet with delegates from the legislatures of the sponsor nations of NATO, with a view to discussing their closer co-operation within the framework of the United Nations organization, the government should give consideration to the acceptance of the invitation.
It will be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the invitation referred to in the resolution would be one that would be addressed to the parliament of Canada, It would not, I suppose, be appropriate for the government, as such, to reply to an invitation of that kind which would be addressed to parliament. In fact, if we did so we might very well be accused of some of these undesirable attitudes in relation to parliament which were thrown at us today by the official opposition, the leader of which is not at present in the house. Nor I believe is the external affairs spokesman of the opposition who would normally be interested in a resolution of this kind. They are no doubt engaged elsewhere on business of vital public importance. I would not for a moment accuse them of being "rude" to the house because they are not here at this time.
I believe it is quite proper, however, that someone in the government should say a few words about a resolution of this kind which deals with such a vitally important matter, even though the invitation referred to in the resolution would be one addressed to parliament. As a matter of fact, an invitation similar to that which has been suggested in the resolution was, I believe, addressed to parliament not so long ago in respect of a meeting of the Council of Europe at Strasbourg. The parliament, not the government, through the Speaker decided to send representatives to that meeting. I believe that was done, and quite properly. As a member of the government who would normally be particularly interested in a matter of this kind, I would think it would be impossible however to state in advance that the members of the government, as such, in discussion with members of their own party, would pledge themselves to the acceptance of any such invitation. I am sure the hon. member who proposed the resolution would agree that we would want to know the source of the invitation, and we would want to know something about the form in which it was couched.
This resolution does not give-I am not complaining about it because it would

probably be impossible to produce a resolution which would do so-any details about the kind of invitation, whether it would be from a government or from an unofficial organization. Nor does it indicate the nature of the invitation. If, however, an invitation came from a responsible governmental source, and the hon. member who moved the resolution has suggested that possibly that responsible source might be the government of Canada, and was couched in proper terms which did not commit those who accepted it to a course of action that might be undesirable, I would think very serious consideration should be given to it, not only by the members of the government but by all the members of the house to whom it would be properly addressed as the parliament of Canada. I do not think I could or should go further than that at this time. I know that any serious proposal which would increase the co-operation of the members of NATO within the framework of the United Nations, as this resolution suggests, and which would thereby strengthen NATO, is one which should commend itself to all the members of this house as I am sure it would commend itself to the members of the government.
From that point of view, it is very easy for me to support the idea behind this resolution. I would not, however, wish that support to be interpreted later on as meaning that an invitation of any kind to the parliament of Canada to participate in a meeting of this kind would, normally and naturally, be approved by the government as such. I have had something to do with the development of NATO, and anyone who has had anything to do with that development cannot help but support any move which would strengthen co-operation between the members of NATO, and by "co-operation" within the meaning of this resolution I am not thinking so much of military co-operation as of co-operation in other fields. There is no member of NATO who is more interested in that kind of co-operation than Canada.

subtopic: CO-OPERATION AMONG SPONSOR NATIONS OP NATO
speechtext: What does the minister mean by that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CO-OPERATION AMONG SPONSOR NATIONS OP NATO
speechtext:
Co-operation in the field of foreign policy; I mean co-operation in the field of economic policy; I mean, as this resolution would seem to indicate, co-operation which would bring NATO and its policies into closer contact with the legislatures of the other countries. That is one of the things most on the mind of the hon. gentleman who has moved this resolution, and that is a question which has already been

discussed by NATO, ways and means by which the organization could be brought closer to parliament.
Hon. members will recall a committee which has been referred to in this house before, the committee of five on non-military co-operation. This committee made a report to the council at Rome and the council at Lisbon. This report was the result of a good deal of examination by a working group presided over by a Canadian official who will shortly be a member of our permanent delegation to NATO. In that report to the council of NATO at Rome, these words were included in the section on possible relations between parliamentary representatives and NATO:
The suggestion that some form of association of parliamentary representatives with certain phases of NATO activity would be desirable was put forward in the committee chiefly with a view to developing an adequate understanding in parliaments and among the general public of NATO and its objectives, and of the role which parliamentary representatives might play in strengthening and developing the North Atlantic community.
No definite proposals were put forward as to how such an association might be developed. It was noted that the Council of Europe includes parliamentary representatives of most North Atlantic countries, but that it also includes certain other countries. It was suggested that some form of closer association of parliamentarians from North Atlantic countries might be developed within the framework of the North Atlantic community, and that possibly parliamentary advisers might be attached to the North Atlantic council delegations.
On the other hand, it was generally recognized by the committee that the problems which have arisen in the relationships between the ministerial and parliamentary organs, for example, in the Council of Europe, would apply equally to any similar arrangements in the NATO context . . . Difficulties might also arise in certain countries whose constitutional arrangements were based upon the principle of the separation of powers, and in countries in whose parliaments there were communist elements of substantial importance. The opinion was also expressed that the establishment of a council of governments in itself provides for the participation of cabinet ministers in various fields who take the responsibility of presenting NATO programs and objectives to their respective parliaments, although it was noted that in the case of at least one North Atlantic country, cabinet ministers were not directly in contact with the legislature and could not assume this responsibility.
Then the report goes on:
It is the opinion of the committee that this is a subject-
That is, closer parliamentary association with NATO.
-which can best be dealt with on the basis of experience and that no general recommendations can be made at this time. It should be examined further at a later date, in the light of the constitutional and political problems involved for each of the North Atlantic governments and the experience of other international bodies.
At our Lisbon meeting, in our report we included a recommendation that that subject
United Nations
should be one of the matters to be gone into by the permanent council, the council which is now sitting in permanent session.

The whole question of economic co-operation within NATO was touched on in previous statements I have made and is now the subject of examination by the NATO agencies concerned. I pointed out previously, and I do not think it would be inappropriate to mention it again now, that in dealing with economic co-operation within NATO we, as members of that organization, have to be careful not to introduce arrangements which would cut across arrangements already made between the members of larger organizations. After all, there are some of the members of NATO who belong to other associations, and all of them belong to the United Nations. We have to be quite certain that, in attempting to reduce the barriers to trade within the NATO group, we shall not be confusing and making more complex arrangements in the larger groups. However, that is all I should like to say about that particular subject at this moment.
On the question of closer parliamentary association, I myself think this is a most desirable objective to be achieved, but it is not always easy to see how it can be done. I am not sure that the procedure of parliamentary advisers which has worked well, I think, with regard to the United Nations, would be equally satisfactory with regard to the NATO council. Certainly in the NATO council meetings I have attended, a good many of the discussions have been in military committee, and a great deal of the information given there was highly secret. Although that fact would not necessarily make the attendance of any member of parliament inadvisable or undesirable-in fact it might make it more desirable-nevertheless there are represented in NATO some governments who would be highly embarrassed indeed if parliamentary representatives of larger

United Nations
groups were invited to be parliamentary-advisers at NATO council meetings.
I am not going to say much more about the resolution now. I do not wish at this time to get into a discussion of how far we should go, not in giving up our sovereignty but in pooling our sovereignty and making it work for us. I have stated in this house and outside of it that, in this day of complicated international relationships, it is obviously desirable, as I see it, to pool our sovereignty with other friendly states in the interests not only of our security but possibly of our survival. Every time we make a mutual aid treaty with any other country we are, in a technical sense, giving up some of our sovereignty, some control over our own affairs, but we are doing that of our own free will in the interests of our own security and of our own prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to apologize to the house because I am afraid I am forced to take part in a debate tonight for which I am not quite ready. I just returned to the city late this afternoon, after some days' absence, and found this resolution was to be debated. I hope I shall be able to make my position lucid and clear, because I would not want any of the hon. members to be under any misapprehension as to where I stand.
The resolution we are debating was introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), and reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, if an invitation is received by the parliament of Canada to appoint delegates to meet with delegates from the legislatures of the sponsor nations of NATO, with a view to discussing their closer co-operation within the framework of the United Nations Organization, the government should give consideration to the acceptance of the invitation.
Before proceeding further may I congratulate the hon. member upon his introductory speech. I thought it was lucid and eloquent, and that it set before the house this afternoon in clear terms exactly what is in the hon. member's mind with respect to future developments on a world scale. In

anything I have to say tonight I wish to assure hon. members, and particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North, that I do not intend to descend into the use of any personalities, or to place my presentation on anything but the highest possible level, because I think the hon. member's resolution is worthy of consideration by all thinking men.
However, the hon. member did admit that his resolution, as it appears at page 9 of today's order paper, is a compromise resolution. Hon. members will recall that on February 26, 1951, the same hon. member moved a resolution in these terms:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of supporting the calling of a convention of delegates from the democracies which sponsored the North Atlantic treaty and representing the principal political parties of such democracies, for the purpose of exploring how far their peoples, and the peoples of such other democracies as the convention may invite to send delegates, can apply among them, within the framework of the United Nations, the principles of federal union.
Hon. members will notice that in the resolution now before the house no mention whatever is made of federal union; but in the mover's address this afternoon I thought he made it clear that, actually, what he seeks is at least a first step toward, if not merely an Atlantic federal union, then perhaps a world federal union.
Hon. members will also be aware of the fact that it was not just on February 26, 1951, that this idea was presented in this parliament. Streit who is the editor of a magazine called Freedom and Union. I have a definite and straightforward purpose in doing that, to show that today what we are actually debating is not whether we shall just call a meeting to discuss how far it is possible for the member nations of NATO to co-operate more fully under article 2 of the treaty but to see how far it would be possible for us to arrange to take the first step toward a fully integrated federal union of the NATO nations and, secondly, to use that as the ramp to catapult us into a wider federal world union. To substantiate that I turn to page 2 of the issue of December 1951 of Freedom and Union. The policy advocated by Mr. Streit and his organization is as follows:
To educate the public, in the U.S. and abroad, in the principles of individual freedom and federal union, and their importance to peace, production, higher living standards and greater spiritual development and happiness.

United Nations
To this end, to support the convocation now of a federal constitutional convention representing all the experienced civil liberty democracies, with a view to their forming a federal union of the free, or Atlantic union, which would guarantee their bill of rights, govern them in those fields where they agree that a common government, federally proportionate to the people, and directly elected by and responsible to them, would best advance their individual freedom, and uphold the right of each nation in the union to continue to govern all its other national affairs in complete independence.
This is the part which is quite enlightening to most of us:
To make sure that such a union shall be formed as the nucleus-the first step toward a universal free federal world government-and shall meanwhile be a loyal member of the United Nations and seek to extend the union's free federal institutions to other nations peacefully and as rapidly as practicable.
To provide a magazine forum for the presentation of all views on the whole problem of freedom and federalism.
It is quite clear that what we are dealing with is not a minor proposition put before us in this resolution. I believe that all of us could quite easily agree that it would be desirable for the free nations of the world and more particularly, now that reference has been made to them, for the NATO nations to convocate at some date representatives of their people to discuss how far it might be possible for them to more fully co-operate for the general good of those nations, for the general good of the world, for the keeping of the peace and that sort of thing. Those are noble ideals and I subscribe to them. I have no objection to going as far as the minister of external affairs suggested this afternoon namely, pooling our sovereignties, using that pool for the common good, especially in times of difficulty such as we are facing today, or in times of crisis.
But I want it understood, as I tried to make it understood by a little interjection this afternoon, that in any pooling of sovereignties that we might arrange, even to meet crises such as we now face, I think it is desirable and in the interests of the liberties of the people to make sure that when they contract in they can also contract out. That is the principle by which I stand, the right to contract out of any international obligation if conditions become intolerable for us in that international arrangement. Otherwise there is no guarantee that we shall ever be able to maintain and preserve our liberties.
So I am quite in accord with the minister and I think with the wording of the resolution, but I believe that everyone who followed the hon. member's introductory speech this afternoon saw that it really was not that that he was debating. But the question I have to ask myself is this: Is it possible that the formation of an Atlantic federation, in which we as individual nations surrender our sovereignty, could bring peace? That is a question we have to ask ourselves. What evidence have we that it would bring peace?
Let us go one step further and look at the end which the world federal unionists have in their minds, the achievement of a world federated state. Let us take that proposition first and look at it. Is it possible that the achievement of a world federated state, with world citizenship and all these glorious things that its advocates envision attached to such a state, will ensure peace to the world? The first thing I have-

to ask myself is whether it would be possible in the first place to achieve a world state. Let us debate that proposition for a minute. What does history tell us? I think history shows that the nearest thing we have ever had to a world state was the holy Roman empire which in my judgment was neither holy, Roman nor an empire, though that is what they called it. There were three things that struck me about the holy Homan empire and that I have always remembered. The first thing is that it was created as a consequence of a long drawn out series of military conquests, and in no other way. That tells me something. Second, the holy Roman empire maintained itself only by further continuous military expeditions that had to be undertaken to put down revolutions and enforce peace. It was never at peace. The third thing that I learned from history was that in the end the holy Roman empire, so-called, broke up with a crash that plunged the whole world into darkness, and not only that, but into a perpetual succession of bandit wars that lasted for many, many years.
What kind of price was paid for that form of world government? I think that the objective that the federal unionists say they want to achieve, world peace, is a worthy objective. I should like to see that world peace established, but I believe we must all be fully aware of the price we shall have to pay for it if we seek it through federal union.
I am wondering if it will be worth the price we shall have to pay for it. There is no guarantee in the world that, even if we pay the terrible price we may have to pay to set up a world federated state, it would bring peace. My judgment tells me it would not.

What the world government advocates refuse to see, as far as I have been able to make out in my study of their proposals, is that no federal union or world state is ever likely to be created, or maintained after it is created, except by force, the force of one very powerful state imposing its will upon the others or the force of a group of states attempting to impose their will upon the others. Is that what my hon. friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North, would call peace? That is not my definition of peace. Let us never forget that the international communist party and the bolshevik leaders of Soviet Russia are determined to create a world state on the model of the Soviet union. No one who knows anything about history can deny
United Nations
that. Lenin held, and he handed down to his successors in the politburo, the conviction that the Marxist state never could live side by side and in peace with the capitalist state. They believe that and they conduct themselves as if they believe it.
At the same time the Russian communist imperialists are logical enough to know that the world state which they promote can never be achieved, can never come into existence, through universal voluntary agreement. That is why they keep huge standing armies and are hastening to build navies and air forces. They know it will have to be imposed by subversion first, undermining the existing order by subversive action in all countries, and then through the use of external armed forces after the subversive activity has done its deadly work. They know that, and that is why they are making preparations as they have been for the time when they will have to resort to all-out armed conflict in order to impose their form of social, legal and economic organization upon the world. I am convinced that no world state could possibly be created before the United States of America and the Soviet union have slugged it out and one of them emerged as the victor and the other as the vanquished; until the victor of that mammoth struggle has imposed his particular social order on the other.
These two are acknowledged to be the powerful world forces, and everybody recognizes that they stand irreconcilable with respect to what kind of social, legal and economic order the world state should have when it is finally achieved. Is it possible, therefore, I ask, to achieve a world government or a federated world state without armed conflict? If not, why is there all this foolish talk about the aim of federal union being the maintenance of peace? If a conflict should occur with these mastodons I have mentioned as the main contenders, would it be possible to get along and have any peace without having the resulting world state policed constantly and perpetually by millions of armed men? That is a question we have got to answer.
What would happen to individual freedom in such a contingency? Can anyone imagine that he would be more free than now? Yet we hear the advocates of federal union say: Surrender some of your freedom now and get bigger freedom later. Before I consent to surrender any sovereignty and freedom I am going to know to whom it is going and what they are going to use it for. Human freedom in a world state today would be suppressed just as surely as darkness follows day. Not only that, I have asked myself
