United Nations
what would happen to world culture. It is a good thing to have different cultures and traditions. Those are the things that make for variety and spice in life. Under a world state brought about as it would have to be today, or perhaps for that matter at any time, I am satisfied the result would be a levelling down of human cultures, because a culture is a mark of differentiation. In the conflict that inevitably would result from the drive to establish a world union or world state today, I cannot imagine that state tolerating too many differences among the people. The idea would be to level down those cultures and make them one. That is not my idea of abundant living and freedom. Any really serious effort to establish a world state today would undoubtedly destroy a good many of the cultures of the world, and any marked differentiation would not be tolerated in such a state. I recall something written by a great writer whose name escapes me for the moment, and I quote it because I agree so much with what he had to say:
The plain reality is that the world, in terms of culture, civilization and consciousness is not and cannot be one world. And to try to make it one, against all the realities of life and nature, is far more likely to awake a spirit of rebellion than the spirit of harmony.
In my opinion the surest way to bring open world conflict is to launch a serious, determined all-out drive for a federated world state. When I say that I also want to ask this question. I do so seriously, without any attempt to throw a cloud over anybody and certainly no one in this house. If it is a fact that -a serious attempt to establish a world state today would plunge us into world conflict, is it not possible that evil forces who know this may try to use a drive for world union to plunge us into a world war? That is one of the things I have to ask myself and which every responsible member of this house will have to ask. No one can deny that there are evil forces who are determined to bring open conflict because they benefit from it. Certainly they will make use of any possible spark to ignite the conflagration.
I think that is all I wish to say about the major proposition. In my judgment it will only be possible for peace to exist in this world under the rule of the divine Son of God, certainly not under the rule of an international junta of power maniacs; and I am not prepared to surrender my sovereignty to such a junta. I am concerned in the main, Mr. Speaker, about preserving the freedoms and liberties that have been won over the centuries at such cost in blood and life. The further you remove from the sovereign individual his controlling government, the more difficult it will be for him to preserve his

freedoms. I am jealous of those freedoms, as I think every red-blooded Canadian must be. Under a world federation what would happen to the liberty to take part in our own government; what would happen to our liberty to worship Almighty God in our own way in our own churches, unmolested? Who is going to say my right will be preserved inviolate? The hon. member for Winnipeg North says the Atlantic union parliament will make laws. Certainly they will; but the mere making of laws is not going to secure to me in perpetuity the right to those freedoms I now hold dear.
When I speak of the freedom to worship Almighty God without molestation in my own way and in my own church, my mind goes to some other people in the world who were convinced that if they surrendered a little of their sovereignty their freedom would be enlarged. I am thinking, for example, of the people of Hungary, who at one time valued very highly their religious liberty. I wonder if their freedom was enlarged when they became a member of the ring of iron states? Ask them today. Think about Cardinal Mina-szenty and some of the others. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that when we think in terms of world government we have to think of those things we hold most dear. In any government, no matter what it is, we have to see that checks and balances are established which will preserve our freedoms inviolate.
Well, if world government cannot guarantee us peace, how in the world can, anyone by any stretch of the imagination say that the complete integration of the economies and politics of the governments of the NATO nations can guarantee us peace? I should say one of the surest ways to guarantee war today would be to go all-out in the formation of an Atlantic federation with the idea of building up terrific strength to match that of the people in the other half of the world. It means that we are getting ready for the conflict, that we really believe it is coming. I have never seen any evidence that you cannot achieve by a treaty of co-operation as much as you could possibly achieve towards establishing peace in the world by a complete political and economic integration of the NATO countries.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North mentioned what I have heard so many people mention when trying to defend their views with respect to federal union. He mentioned that the United States had achieved a very workable form of government by federal union. He further said the Atlantic federal union would be exactly similar. I do not think he went quite as far as some others have gone, but I just want to point out something that a lot of people conveniently do not

remember. I have in my hand a clipping from the New York American of February 28, 1951. The writer unfortunately did not append his name to the article, but it hits the nail so much on the head that I want to put small parts of it on the record. This contains a comparison of the so-called NATO federal union or Atlantic union with what happened in the United States of America. The heading of this article is, "A dishonest parallel." The article reads:
George Washington, who held as one of his deepest convictions that the United States could survive only by avoiding foreign entanglements, is now quoted by advocates of world government in support of their strange proposal.
In the course of the constitutional convention, in 1787, General Washington wrote to a friend complaining that the reluctance of the individual states to surrender their sovereignty to a federal government was keeping the nation "weak, inefficient and disgraceful."
The letter has been cited by Lawrence Dawson, executive director of the United World Federalists of Illinois, as an argument in favour of his organization's proposal that this nation yield its sovereignty to a world government.
"Although General Washington was referring to the states which became the United States of America," said Mr. Dawson, "the principle of delegating sovereignty to which he referred is precisely the same principle which the United World Federalists hope to see applied through the United Nations to the entire world.
"In that limited field necessary to abolish war, we federalists believe that the world should be governed by the same system of carefully delineated and delegated central authority which has worked so magnificently ... in our country."
Now, the writer says this, and it is very much to the point.
This is a monstrous argument. It rests on the pretense that the United States would have no more to lose in yielding its sovereignty to a world government than had each of the states in yielding to a central government created by themselves.
But the utter dishonesty of that pretense is evident at a glance.
The inhabitants of the thirteen states were all Americans.
They had local differences but they shared, all of them, the basic idea that individual liberty was the most important thing on earth, and that the only way it could be preserved was through self-government by the people.
Only if that same ideal were passionately shared by all the peoples of the world would the parallel which one-world advocates try to draw between the thirteen American states of 1787 and the nations of the earth today be accurate or honest.
I agree.
The greater part of the earth is inhabited by backward masses who have no understanding of liberty, or so much as even a dream of liberty.
And among many of the more advanced peoples the ideal of freedom, where if it survives at all, is greatly diluted.
Some have permitted themselves to be enslaved to dictatorships; others have traded off their liberties for socialism's false promises of security.
When the Messiahs of the one-world daydream suggest that America could submit to the control of nations that do not know freedom without sacrificing its own freedom, they are saying, therefore, something that simply is not true.

There is no parallel, Mr. Speaker, between what happened in the United States or what happened in Canada and what would happen in the attempt to set up Atlantic federal union or world federal union.
I think one valid argument that was used by the hon. member was that some form of Atlantic union is necessary to ensure control of the military by civil government. I believe that. I agree that his argument there was valid. Certainly, we must never allow ourselves to become in any way subject to the rule of a military junta. For that reason I am sympathetic to the idea of some kind of very close co-operation, but on a basis that would allow every nation to contract out if the conditions under which they have to work become intolerable, to see to it that a civil administration that could control the military is set up.
I agree further with my hon. friend when he says that we must do everything we can to make article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty work. Surely, his argument is sound on that. I must say, and I say this in conclusion because I know my time is running out, that the general assumption that communism spreads only throughout countries or amongst peoples who are hungry and have a lower standard of living, cannot be substantiated.

Mr. Speaker, last year, as has been mentioned, a somewhat similar resolution was presented here in the House of Commons. At that time I was not present. I was a member of a group in Winnipeg that was watching for that debate with considerable interest, as were several other groups in all the major cities across Canada. To our disappointment the debate collapsed with only the mover of the resolution, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) taking part.
The subject matter of this particular resolution is of very considerable interest and importance to many people in Canada, and it is desirable that several members participate in the debate, as has happened on this occasion, because there are various points of view to be set forward. I do not propose advocating world government; for my thinking has not carried me that far. I propose, however, supporting the resolution for reasons that follow.
We face two great problems which overshadow all our internal troubles and disputes: The problem of defence preparedness so that we may not lose our freedom, and the problem of finding a way towards enduring peace.
The energy that we devote to strengthening our defences must be matched by the energy we display in exploring every road, every path or even faintly marked trail, that leads toward peace. General Eisenhower has expressed the thoughts of millions in some of his remarks which John Gunther quoted in the Ottawa Citizen of April 25. These are General Eisenhower's words:
Total war would be the suicide of our generation.
We must train the youth of America to avert world war III, and not to refight world war II.
There is no glory in battle worth the blood it costs.
I hate war as only a soldier who has lived it can.
Weakness cannot co-operate with anything. We have got to be strong.
I hold that a resolute, intelligent, and frankly displayed determination to live up to our present position in the world is vital to our current and future welfare.
It is with those thoughts in mind that I approach the present subject. The importance of this motion before us is that it concentrates attention upon the problem that should be uppermost in the minds of all people, namely, can democracy survive in this era of world revolution? For we are living in a period of revolution just as important as any revolutionary period in history.
The threat of the present crisis is towards the liberty and freedom of the citizens of the democracies. I think that it is wise sometimes to look back into history, and my excursion shall be very brief. I was reading just the other day some debates of the House of Commons at Westminster dealing with army estimates. One of the hon. members there was stressing the development of weapons from the earliest times, and had reached the middle ages when he was interrupted by an hon. member on the opposite side who said: "On a point of order; are we discussing the war estimates of William the Conqueror, or what?" The Speaker intervened and said, in a kindly fashion, "I think the honourable and learned member was advancing cautiously but steadily towards the present age." I will advance a little more speedily in my review of some earlier history.
I think we should remember that democracy, as a form of government, has a very short history, when compared with other forms of government. The history of the world has shown that political power has been longer in the hands of autocrats and oligarchs than in the hands of the people. In the ancient world democratic government arose in the states of Greece, and persisted for about four hundred years. It flourished in the fifth century B.C., declined in the fourth under the Macedonian conquest, revived in feebler form after the death of Alexander the Great, and perished under the weight of the Roman empire.
Centuries elapsed before democracy was re-established. The last three hundred years have witnessed the modern flowering of democratic government. But the threat of Russian imperialism is as grave now for the democracies of today as were the threats of Sparta and of the autocrat Philip of Macedon to the democracies of Ancient Greece. They perished for the same reasons that threaten us now-lack of cohesion and of political unity. Their military alliances proved unstable. Their preparations for war were

United Nations
delayed. Their policies were as well known to the enemy as to themselves, for they were debated in public. Their ranks were infiltrated by enemy sympathizers. They lacked unity of purpose. They fell, one by one, to the aggressor, although their combined strength effectively asserted would have saved them.
War may not be inevitable, but the history of the world discloses very few periods when it has not been afflicting mankind. The only long period of peace enjoyed by western Europe occurred in the first and second centuries A.D. when the Roman empire was supreme and the legions kept the barbarians in check beyond the frontiers. Several generations of men in Europe lived in freedom from the fear of war.
Their successors have not been so fortunate. No similar peaceful period was seen again until the nineteenth century, when the British fleet and the Monroe doctrine effectively discouraged any maritime adventures. The twentieth century has experienced the most devastating wars in the long and troubled history of mankind with destruction and atrocities reminiscent of Genghis Khan or of the thirty years' war.
The one compelling desire of twentieth century man is for relief from this recurring disaster. With the rapid development of the means of destruction the need for a solution to the problem of world war preoccupies our thoughts and calls for the most earnest and active measures, if civilization is not to receive a mortal blow.
Arnold Toynbee in his book "Civilization on Trial" shows clearly that we have no grounds for belief that our civilization will endure forever. During the last five or six thousand years many civilizations, he points out, have risen, have declined and have fallen. In that period of six thousand years, democracy, which gives the greatest freedom to the individual, is a form of government that has had much the briefest history. We consider it man's highest achievement in government. Can it be maintained unimpaired, safe from the foes without and the perils within?
Toynbee suggests that we are not doomed to make history repeat itself; that it is open to us through our own efforts to give history a new and unprecedented turn. He considers that we have three tasks-in politics, to establish a constitutional co-operative system of world government; in economics, to find working compromises between free enterprise and socialism; and in the life of the spirit, to put the secular superstructure back on to religious foundations. Of these three tasks the political task is the most urgent. The

world is on the eve of being unified politically by one means or another. Can we stave off unification by force?
Efforts towards peace have been very great. During the nineteenth century over 400 peace organizations were formed, distributed among 15 countries, and more than a hundred international peace congresses were held. In the twentieth century we have seen many alliances formed, many peace treaties signed. We had a league of nations for twenty years, attempting to obtain security for the nations of the world by means of conference. A similar attempt has been made through the United Nations. A successful solution still seems far distant. Precarious peace is being maintained in some areas of the world now by the age-old methods of treaties, alliances and collective security measures. None of these methods in the past has prevented the outbreak of war.
Before attempting to make plans for the prevention of world war it would seem necessary to determine the causes of war. That is no easy task, for there are as many opinions as there are men who have discussed the matter. I attempted a few years ago to summarize the causes that have been advanced by leading individuals to account for the outbreak of the wars which the common people do not want. They are as follows: The natural pugnacity of mankind; economic conditions, the revolt of the have-nots against the haves; the special wickedness of a people; the imperialistic ambitions of nations; revenge for earlier defeats or for unredressed grievances; fear of encirclement; the conscious wickedness of governments, rulers, diplomats, capitalists and imperialists; the selfishness of men; the struggle of oppressed subject peoples; the activities of armament manufacturers; the breakdown of international trade; the battle for oil, raw materials and markets, and the international financiers.
Another cause was given by the late Lord Lothian, who was British ambassador to the United States in 1939, who said:
The fundamental cause of war Is neither unjust treaties, nor racial or religious or cultural differences, nor maltreatment of minorities, nor need for raw materials and markets, nor imperialist ambitions, nor strategic considerations, nor capitalism or nationalism. The cause of war is the anarchy of sovereign states. The end of war can come only through world federation.
There are others who consider that despite all our efforts the only hope for the future lies in a change in the minds and hearts of men such as Christianity can bring about through its emphasis on love and brotherhood. Lord Lothian suggested that although that is true in so far as the final abolition of war is concerned, nevertheless it is the function of politics and government to create the practical

conditions in which resort to violence will be forbidden and prevented between nations, as it is now between individuals and groups within national states.
These views give some idea of the diversity of opinion concerning the cause of war and the complexity of the problem. Unless agreement can be reached as to the cause of war it will be difficult to formulate measures to prevent war. If Lord Lothian's view be accepted that the root cause of war is anarchy, what steps are necessary to replace the present anarchy with the rule of international law? There are sixty sovereign states within the world, each a law unto itself. Because each nation is a law unto itself the secondary causes of war frequently prevail to disturb the peace of the world-the ambition of rulers, fear of encirclement and so forth.
It is obvious that sovereignty might be maintained unimpaired if the nations would of their own accord accept arbitration for the settlement of their disputes. That method is well known to Canada, the United States and Great Britain for it was thus that our boundary disputes were settled. Among the great nations of the world arbitration has been resorted to on more than two hundred occasions in the period from 1794 to 1914. It has never been accepted as a compulsory method of settling differences.
The league of nations offered a method for solving international disputes but it soon became clear that some states were not disposed to abide by the decisions of the league and preferred to withdraw from that organization. The present United Nations has disappointed in part the hopes of its founders.
Within the last thirty-seven years we have had two world wars, a league of nations and a United Nations and are now -back to the old and oft-tried plan of alliance and coalition. Now it is the United States and her allies against Russia and her allies and satellites. Earlier it was Athens against Sparta, Rome against Carthage, Marlborough, Eugene and Holland against Louis XIV, the *Grand Alliance against Napoleon, the Triple Entente against the Triple Alliance. Thus does history repeat itself and the prevention of world war seems as distant as ever.
As Sebastian Haffner puts it in the London Observer and as repeated in the Globe and Mail of November 26, 1951:
In our historical experience, coalitions are shortlived and ephemeral structures. They are knocked together for the purpose of war against a common enemy, and they regularly fall apart as soon as the war and the common danger are over; or, if the expected war does not materialize, they disintegrate quietly.
The great coalition, which is embodied in the North Atlantic treaty, has from its inception been
United Nations
meant to defy this historical law. Whatever Russian propaganda may say, it never was an alliance for war; its purpose was and is to prevent war and to enforce and maintain peace. This is a long-term aim and it means that the coalition must hold together as a working organization over a long term of years and maintain joint policies in spite of the many disruptive factors which are bound to arise between sovereign allies in the course of time.
Maintaining a coalition during the course of a war is difficult enough. A military disaster, a change of government, internal troubles

any one of these or other causes may result in the loss of an ally. Recall the difficulties that faced the allies in 1917-a military reverse in Italy, disaffection and mutiny in the French army, revolution in Russia. Only the aid and steadfastness of Britain and the United States saved the situation on the western front. In a protracted cold war period which is the endless vista before us there is the gravest danger that some of the partners might become weary of the struggle and withdraw into isolation or be weakened economically and become an easy prey to a fifth column.
Even the strongest member of the present coalition presents a problem. Bruce Hutchison writing in Maclean's, April 1 of this year, has this to say:
The United States is trying to erect and lead, in a fashion never known on earth before, a worldwide coalition of free peoples whom it does not understand and frequently antagonizes through its lack of understanding.
The biggest question of all-
He quotes a leading United States government figure as saying:
-is whether a democracy under our system, and with our anti-military tradition, can build up enough power for the job, and, if it does so, whether it can maintain that power for years, maybe decades, without either using it recklessly or getting tired of the load and dissolving it, just as the Russians hope. It'll be the toughest thing we ever tackled and remember, if you foreigners need our understanding, we'll need yours.
Is the answer to this and to other problems that face the North Atlantic Treaty Organization a form of political union among the various members? The objective before us seems to have two features, one the maintenance of peace if possible by such preparations that any aggressor will be restrained from running the risk of war and, secondly, if war does occur, that the western democracies will be so strong and so united that victory in the struggle will be assured.
Some form of political union between the members of the great coalition seems essential. The differences of race do not constitute an insuperable barrier. North American man is merely western European man transplanted across the Atlantic. There are thousands and hundreds of thousands of North Americans

United Nations
whose birthplace was in western Europe and millions who are descendants of western Europeans. An Atlantic community of democratic peoples numbering over 300 millions needs only the closer bonds of political union to form a unity that would be proof against the ambition of any foreign power. In that Atlantic community is contained the industrial might and power of western civilization. In that Atlantic community, united and strong and free, would be preserved the great spiritual heritage of western civilization and of Christianity.
The motion for consideration before us does not commit either the government or Canada in any way. It merely suggests that the way be kept open for consultation and investigation. Our goal is peace with honour. Our hope is for freedom and for security from the scourge of war. Closer co-operation between the sponsor nations of NATO may be the road to enduring peace. We should explore that road or any other so that we may satisfy ourselves that no effort has been spared. Vision and faith are needed in this hour if our civilization is to survive.

speechtext:
There are a few words I should like to say in closing the debate. First of all, I am glad that at least three other members partook in it this year. Perhaps we shall have even more next year when some similar motion again comes before the house. What I should now like to do, however, is to clarify some of the matters which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) raised this afternoon. AS' he pointed out, and as is of course the case, one cannot include every possible aspect of the situation within a resolution such as this without making it most cumbersome. The points he raised were valid and I find myself in complete agreement with them. Indeed, were I to rewrite the resolution with all points in it I would be perfectly willing to state that we should not accept an invitation to such a conference unless it came from one of the governments of the seven sponsor nations of NATO.
Second, I would assume that such an invitation would imply that there was a responsible purpose behind the invitation. Third, the whole purpose of my concept of union would be destroyed were members of parliament to go to such a conference with power to pledge the Canadian government to a certain course of action. Those whom I should like to see

go to such a conference are parliamentarians on their own as parliamentarians and therefore in no way able to commit the government.
Perhaps with these matters cleared up the Secretary of State for External Affairs might feel able to accept the resolution, weak in some ways though I think it is. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has just told me that he hopes to be able to say a few words on his resolution. Therefore I shall be very brief in what I have to say. I should like to comment much more fully upon the interesting and informative speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) but time precludes. As for the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I listened to him with interest but he always seems to me to have an infinite capacity for reducing his own views to absurdity.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) gave us a very interesting contribution but I thought he was chasing intellectual hares. He quoted the New York American with some relish but I assume he has not seen recent copies of the Chicago Tribune which really outdo the American considerably. In fact the resident Ottawa correspondent of the Chicago Tribune recently wrote to his paper implying that certain United States senators were coming to Ottawa to sell out their country. I assure the hon. member for Peace River that if he follows the Tribune closely he will find a great deal of ammunition against us Atlantic unionists but of course most of it would be completely erroneous. I think the hon. member for Peace River was arguing against something for which I was not arguing. I was discussing the proposition of federal union throughout the world. I do not think world government is a practical proposition today but I do think by some form of union we could appreciably strengthen NATO. The hon. member for Peace River asks for an alliance into which we can contract and out of which we can contract. Per contra, our allies could contract out of that alliance just as rapidly as we could, and there would simply be no security of any sort whatsoever with such a loose conglomeration of nations ready to get out when the going got tough.
I am an Atlantic unionist. I should like to see these seven nations brought together very closely, and I should like to see it done without benefit of war. As I said this afternoon, if war comes, survival will demand that we enter into that form of union. But I was only arguing for Atlantic union. Obviously we are not going to get it within the predictable future. Therefore I am prepared to compromise to a substantial extent on my

views in the hope of creating something stronger than we have now. I believe Atlantic union amongst these seven nations would give us power so great that any potential aggressor would think several times before he attacked us. After all, wars today are not only won on the field of battle. They are won principally in the factories. They are won by industrial potential, and these seven countries together would control almost 70 per cent of the world's industrial potential. With that behind us we should be in an extraordinarily strong position, strong enough, I suggest, to offer the best hope for escape from the scourge of war.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCREASE AMOUNTS PAID TO COMPENSATE FOR INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
PROPOSAL TO INCREASE AMOUNTS PAID TO COMPENSATE FOR INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation increasing the amounts paid under the Family Allowances Act to the extent necessary to compensate for the increase in the cost of living since the said act was first enacted.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure this evening to move the foregoing resolution.
As hon. members will recall, the Family Allowances Act was enacted on August 5, 1944. It came into operation when the first payments were made in July, 1945. The prime minister of that day, the Right Hon, W. L. Mackenzie King, in introducing the family allowances motion and bill, stated that it was one of the important measures the government was going to take towards post-war reconstruction and the introduction of a new era. I believe the Family Allowances Act has been of great value especially to families in the low income groups. Because of the improvements that have resulted from family allowances by way of better clothing, food and medical care, and improved educational opportunity, all citizens of Canada stand to gain. Benefit has resulted mainly to the children of low income families, but I welcome the fact that family allowances are paid without a means test.
The government can and does recover from those in the higher income brackets a large part of what they receive in family allowances, if not perhaps even more. Family allowances have made an important contribution in improving health standards among
Family Allowances Act our children. I believe they have resulted in children being able to obtain a better education. If young Canadians grow up in better health and receive a better education they will be in a better position to help produce the wealth of this country. If they have been reared in good health and given a more adequate education, in their adult life they will be more productive and consequently the net result to Canada will be a betterment in our standards for generations to come. I believe the family allowance is a good investment in the future, and will pay the nation enormous dividends.
When introducing the legislation the late prime minister, Mr. King, pointed out that in the first six months of 1944 some 39-3 per cent of all those presenting themselves for enlistment for active service were rejected. It was Mr. King's opinion that if the Family Allowances Act had been in operation in the days of the great depression that rejection rate would have been much lower. Family allowance is a good investment if peace is maintained in the years to come. It is an equally good investment if our nation should once more face an emergency such as prevailed in 1944.
I think hon. members will agree that if the Family Allowances Act was good in August, 1944, and if the payments of those days were the payments that should be made under such legislation, those payments do not represent the same purchasing power today. In other words, as the years have gone by the value of the family allowance has been reduced. So I present this motion in the hope that the house may support not a real increase in the value of the family allowance cheque but a restoration of the family allowance to the same purchasing power it possessed in August, 1944. It may be said, as is true, that if this resolution were adopted it would add a substantial sum to our expenditure, and it may be argued we are not in a position to meet such additional payments. I think hon. members should remember that the payment of family allowances is not at all in the same position as, for example, an increased vote for national defence or rearmament. When we spend money on arms we spend it on something that does not go into consumption in Canada and does not improve our standard of living. On the other hand an increase in the family allowance is merely a redistribution of purchasing power among Canadians, and1 I believe it is time low income families were

Family Allowances Act given family allowance cheques which would purchase a great deal more than is the case today.
Then I believe an increase in the family allowance would mean a definite improvement in our home market. Canada is facing a real emergency, not because we cannot produce enough food but because agriculture surpluses are piling up. I do not suppose the Canadian market could absorb all those surpluses, but I am sure that if the government increased family allowances there would be a greater consumption of such food as meat, milk, butter and eggs. People enjoying a high standard of living consume a high protein diet, and it is those very protein foods that are in surplus in Canada today. I believe that by increasing the family allowance we would provide an increased Canadian market for agricultural products.
The government has tried various fiscal measures to control inflation. Apparently inflation has been brought under control, at least temporarily, but inflation in the last few years has been terrific. The price level is up; the cost of living is up. Because of that increase in the cost of living, because inflation has resulted from the failure of the government to take adequate measures, I say there is a responsibility on the government to do what it can to alleviate the inflation that exists today and therefore should restore the value of the family allowance. There has been a small decrease in the cost of living in recent months. There has been a somewhat larger decrease in the wholesale index. Agricultural products are in surplus supply. There is substantial unemployment. Everyone knows that inflation is usually followed by deflation and often by depression. I believe the payment of the family allowance together with the other social security measures we now have in effect, such as the old age pension, in themselves provide a cushion against possible depression. In other words, whether inflation or deflation should come, it is in our best interests to increase the value of the family allowance.
There has been a terrific increase in the cost of living since August, 1944, when this legislation was enacted. At that time the cost of living index stood at 118-9. In March, 1952, it stood at 189-1. There had been an increase in the cost-of-living index within that period of 59 per cent. I am suggesting that the government should increase family allowances to the extent of approximately 60 per cent. I should like to see the minimum monthly payment per child increased from $5 to $8. I should like to see the maximum monthly payment per child increased from $8 to $13, with the other payments varying

accordingly. I say I propose that family allowances should be increased by 60 per cent in order to compensate for the general increase in the cost-of-living index.
I believe that family allowances are spent by the mothers of Canada mainly on clothing and food for the children. The clothing index has increased more than the general cost-of-living index. In August, 1944, the clothing index was 121-5; in March of this year that index was 211-2, an increase of 74 per cent. I say, therefore, that a suggested increase in the family allowance of 60 per cent is a moderate one and is 14 per cent less than the increase in the clothing index since August, 1944. The increase in the food index has been even more substantial. In August, 1944, the food index was 131-5; in March of this year that index was 241-7, an increase in that period of 84 per cent. Surely, a suggested increase of 60 per cent in the family allowance is most moderate, as it is actually 24 per cent less than the increase in the food index.
As I have already stated I suggest a 60 per cent increase in the family allowance because, since 1944, the general cost of living has increased by approximately that amount.
1	believe if the family allowance were increased that increase would be used by the mothers of Canada, almost without exception, to improve the health and nutritional standards of their families. One of the most important commodities for the growing child to receive is milk. Canada can produce lots of milk. We have a surplus of cheese in Ontario now, which is just another form of milk. Our dairy surpluses are threatening the dairy industry, yet statistics show that from 1946 to 1951 there has been a decrease in the consumption of milk in Canada. In 1946 Canadians consumed almost 6,000,000,000 pounds of milk; in 1951 it was 5,865,000,000 or a decrease within that five-year period of
2	per cent. But that does not tell the whole story. From 1941 to 1951 there was an increase in the population of Canada of 18-6 per cent, apart from the population of Newfoundland. A 2 per cent decrease in the actual consumption of milk between 1946 and 1951, therefore, because of the increase in population becomes a greater per capita percentage decrease. I estimate in those five years from 1946 to 1951, because of inflation, because of the high cost of living and the fact that low income groups could not afford to buy all the milk their families needed, milk consumption per capita in Canada dropped by approximately 10 per cent.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the consumption of milk in Canada would increase substantially with an increase in the family

allowance. We have milk in surplus supply. The only thing standing in the way of many thousands of Canadian children receiving more milk is the fact that their parents have not got the money to buy it at present high prices. I believe that an increase in the family allowance would not only allow mothers to buy necessary increased quantities of milk, but would result in the general nutritional standards being raised. It would result in these children being better clothed, receiving better medical care and being given an opportunity for better education.
At the present time we are engaged in a large rearmament program. Democracy throughout the world is being challenged. But if we are to protect democracy in Canada, I do not think we should allow large defence expenditures to stand in the way of maintaining the value of our social security legislation. Real production in Canada is going up year after year. In his speech the other night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) pointed out that within the last year real production in Canada had increased by more than 5 per cent. I do not believe that this resolution of mine really goes far enough. I should, perhaps, be advocating that the real value of the family allowance should be steadily increased. But in the hope that the government will give my proposition more favourable consideration, I have kept my proposal within what I consider moderate bounds.
All I am saying to the government in this resolution is, do not allow defence expenditures or any other claim on budget revenues to stand in the way of protecting the purchasing power of the family allowance, the old age pension or other social security measures. Can Canada afford such an increase today? The increase would amount to approximately $192 million based on the estimated cost of family allowances during this year of $320-5 million. For this year our gross national product is estimated at $22-5 billion. Surely we can afford something less than one per cent for the welfare of Canadian children. Surely, we can afford something less than one per cent of the gross national product in order to restore the purchasing power of the family allowance.
The sum of $5 a month for a child under 6 years of age, $8 a month for a child of 13, 14 or 15 years of age, is not very much. No one expects the government, or the parliament of Canada, to make provision of family allowances to the point necessary to maintain a child in a home. In other words, the parents must have a continuing responsibility. Is $5 a month now, for an infant child, of sufficient
Family Allowances Act help in relation to the cost of keeping that newborn child in health, in comfort and growing satisfactorily?
Perhaps some hon. members, like myself, have purchased the last issue of Life magazine. In that magazine is set out the cost in New York of a layette. As I understand it, a layette consists of all the provisions and equipment that a mother needs for a newborn child, the first child. She needs these provisions to take care of the child when she brings it home from the hospital. In New York it is estimated that the cost of the average layette is $400. This article goes on to point out that the mother, if she budgets very carefully, may provide all of the things necessary to care for her newborn child for the amount of $275. It takes a lot of family allowance cheques to reach the sum of $275. It takes 55 family allowance cheques; it takes almost five years for the present family allowance cheques to total the smallest sum, according to Life magazine, that it is necessary to spend on provisions to take care of a newborn child.
I use that example, Mr. Speaker, to point out that the present family allowance cheque is wholly inadequate. My resolution, I repeat, asks the house to consider not an increase in the real value of family allowances but merely that this house is of the opinion that the purchasing power of the family allowance cheque should be restored.
When family allowances were mentioned in Canada, before the act was passed, it was stated by a lot of people that the provision of family allowance cheques to a percentage of mothers in Canada would result in the cheques being spent on riotous living, and for things other than the benefit of the children in the home. But the statistics that have come from the experience in the Department of National Health and Welfare show that Canadian mothers, almost without exception, spend the family allowance cheques wisely and to the advantage of their children. Children to the number of 2,956,844 were in receipt of family allowances in 1945-46. There were 1,910,192 families in receipt of family allowances in 1950-51. Of almost 2 million families in receipt of family allowances, only 56 prosecutions were under consideration. In other words, Mr. Speaker, only one mother out of every 33,000 mothers in Canada was even suspected of having spent the family allowance cheque unwisely. Therefore I say that the experience of the family allowance branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare is a real tribute to Canadian mothers. Canadian mothers take the family allowance cheques and almost without exception spend them for the welfare of their own children.

Family Allowances Act
By improving the health standards of our children, and by improving educational standards, on becoming adult citizens they will be, because of family allowance legislation, healthier citizens, better educated citizens and will consequently make a better contribution to the welfare of Canada and of the world.
Once again I say that democracy cannot afford to stand still. Our way of life is on trial. It is not good enough for us to mark time on social security measures. It is not even good enough for us to protect the value of social security measures that have been legislated in the past; rather, because of ever increasing production in Canada, our social security legislation should be improved and expanded. Therefore I say to the government the very least we can do in parliament at this time, if we are to keep faith with Canadian motherhood, is to restore the purchasing power of the family allowances.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words only in support of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). On two occasions I suggested to the house that the government could and should increase the amount of family allowances. I have not changed my mind on the matter especially in view of the substantial increase in the cost of living these past few years. It would seem,-and this is fortunate,-that the cost of living is becoming more stable. Nevertheless it is still considerably higher than it was when the government passed this fair family allowances legislation.
The member who preceded me and who moved this resolution stressed the way mothers, in particular, are using the money received in the form of family allowances. I have the privilege of living in the country, while my humble calling puts me, moreover, in daily touch with families of all classes and circumstances.
If I trust my humble experience, I think I may state again, in this house, that our families are putting to excellent use the money these cheques bring them. You can hardly imagine, Mr. Speaker, how happy our mothers are, and how proud even, to use their family allowance cheques in order to furnish their small children with, amongst other things, the medicine and the medical attention they need.
Now, it is possible, and even very probable, that in some cases, though very rarely, there may have been some abuse which only confirms the general rule.
But I repeat that the great majority of our families make proper use of that extra money they receive every month. From the social point of view, I believe nobody can contend that this government investment is not well-advised. Everyone agrees that the family is an essential institution which we must strive to preserve and develop, since the family is still the great reservoir that supplies the nation with its manpower and population increases.
We are counting on immigration to increase the population of Canada. We are not discussing that matter now. May I say though that we should first look to the family to obtain the surplus population needed to develop in our country true Canadian citizens. It is the family that above all will give us true Canadian citizens.

Well, to my mind, family allowances are an excellent means of helping and encouraging our Canadian families. Therefore, it is an excellent piece of legislation both from a social and an economic standpoint.
Once again I say that the increase in the amount of family allowances should not necessarily be of a permanent nature; and so, I would be quite willing to suggest that should the cost of living go down, this increase in the family allowance cheques could be reduced proportionately.
The mover of the resolution has suggested an increase of 60 per cent. That may not be enough. Perhaps we might simply consider doubling the amount of the allowance for the time being, only to reduce it gradually as the cost of living decreases.
In any event, I do not wish to take up too much time. I only wanted to add a few words to those of the mover of the resolution and to say that, in my humble opinion, a splendid opportunity awaits the government of improving an already excellent piece of social legislation which could nevertheless be made even better.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCREASE AMOUNTS PAID TO COMPENSATE FOR INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
I do not quite appreciate the significance of my hon. friend's interjection, but it likely has a significance I do not yet see. We are now spending in Canada about $1,500 million on health and social security measures on the account of federal and provincial governments. The old age security measure which was introduced in parliament at the last session raised our expenditures in the field of social security by over $300 million.
The hon. gentleman may think that all that one has to do is to make a proposal and, because it is meritorious, it should be adopted regardless of the cost. I have never lost an opportunity when speaking about these things -I think my record and indeed that of the government in these matters is no less sincere than that of the hon. gentleman who proposed this resolution-to indicate, as I think we should when discussing such measures, the extent to which we can guarantee their continuance. The money for these measures does not come out of our pockets as a government or out of the pockets of any individual member or group of members of parliament. True, we make our contributions to the general tax fund, but the moneys for all of these measures must come from but one source, the hard work of the Canadian people. There is no other source. Consequently when one comes to consider the desirability of any particular proposal one

must relate it to the capacity of the people, in the light of all the obligations of the government, to meet the cost of the proposal if accepted. That is certainly true of this measure.
We are spending, as I say, $1,500 million this year-the federal government, the provincial governments and voluntary organizations-on health and welfare. The federal government is charged with the responsibility of administering substantially 80 per cent of that figure. I submit that that is a significant sum of money which has to be raised by taxation imposed on the people of this country, on those who represent the class of people who are directly represented in the 84 per cent of the population that have to be maintained by roughly 19 per cent of the working population of the country.
One is often charged in the administration of these measures with being profligate and insensible to the relation between the capacity to pay and the benefits obtained. I deny and the government denies that in the administration of these measures or in the adoption of any of these measures we have been profligate. We have sought at all times, from the Old Age Pensions Act of 1926 up to the present time, to relate our expenditures to the national income, to the national product and generally to the capacity of the nation to meet these obligations.
When one thinks that today we are paying slightly less, in terms of the budget of the nation, on health and welfare than we were in 1938 one cannot be accused of engaging in irresponsible administration. Of course it will be argued, as indeed the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) argued the other night, that if that is the case the country can give consideration to increasing its expenditures, particularly in the field of social security. But in making that suggestion I think the hon. member overlooked the fact that $2,000 million is being budgeted this year for national defence.
That does not represent, we hope, a normal expenditure of government but an expenditure of government which we believe to be desirable at this time in the interests of maintaining decency, and civilization, and making our contribution toward peace by supporting the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We have paid out in family allowances $1,882 million from the inauguration of family allowance payments up to March 31, 1952. As the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution has said, there can be no doubt about the social benefits of this provision. Family allowances undoubtedly, based not upon emotional anticipation but upon actual continuing checks and surveys, have helped Canadian 55704-I06i
Family Allowances Act parents to provide better food, better shelter, better clothing, improved health care and! education for their children. Generally speaking there can be no doubt about these benefits. Therefore I am in full accord with what the hon. gentleman has had to say in that particular, as indeed I am sure is every hon. member of the house.
On the other hand, it is interesting to note that by the time a child reaches the age of 16 we estimate that on the average that child will have received throughout his or her period of life up to the age of 16 something in the neighbourhood of $1,188. That represents a considerable sum of money, particularly for the low income groups. It does give parents an opportunity of doing something for their children which, but for the existence of this measure, they would not be able to do. I think one of the most salutary results of the family allowances measure is that in every one of our provinces since 1945 when the act became effective school attendance has gone up to its highest point and has not receded except for two cases in one year. That is of course a result of the highest value. It is a result that other countries cannot claim largely because there is not the same strictness of administration in some countries as in our own. The moment a child under 16 years ceases attending school in Canada payment is suspended unless an adequate reason for non-attendance .of the child at school is given by the parent responsible or by the person acting in the status of a parent.
The immensity of our program, which now costs us over $300 million a year, may be seen in the following figure. If the United States, for instance, were to adopt a program such as ours it would cost that country $3,500 million a year. It is not for us of course to comment on the existence of legislation in that country, but I think the immensity of our own program is seen in the fact that it would cost almost $31 billion a year if a family allowance measure were adopted in the United States. Therefore, in suggesting as the hon. member did that there should be an increase in the amount paid under the Family Allowances Act, I am sure he would not want to have us interpret his suggestion as meaning that the present plan does not represent a very substantial social measure involving a very substantial sum of money.
The fact is that it does represent the second most costly social venture that this country has undertaken, a venture which in our case is more expensive and more extensive in its financial benefits than the benefits paid under family allowances measures of any other country in the world but one. It is interesting to compare some of our benefits with those in countries where the family allowances
1676	HOUSE OF
Family Allowances Act measure is somewhat comparable. It would have been interesting to have the hon. gentleman indicate how our measure compares with other countries such as New Zealand, Australia or Great Britain. Because they are relative comparisons I should like to give comparative figures at this time. First of all with respect to the total amount spent on family allowances in any one year on a per capita basis, as well of course as the total amount spent since the inauguration of family allowances, Canada leads all countries on the basis of payments as they are at present altogether apart from the proposal of my hon. friend which he says would amount to another $192 million a year.
The percentage of net national income spent on family allowances in New Zealand is 2-65 compared with 2-15 in Canada, but the Canadian figure of 2 [DOT] 15, compared with 1-41 for Australia and -57 for Great Britain, indicates that the Family Allowances Act as it stands with relation to existing benefits represents an amount of money which demonstrates the determination of the people of Canada to provide the most satisfactory family allowances program possible. Likewise it would have been interesting if he had compared the relation of family allowance payments to other social security expenditures. In Canada, for instance, for the year 1951 family allowance expenditures represented 27 -7 per cent of all social security expenditures, taking into account the veterans charter, the Old Age Pensions Act of that day, the national health program, the unemployment insurance measure and various other miscellaneous measures that come within this category. Let us compare that with the proportionate expenditure made in Australia and other countries, that is to say, the relation of family allowance expenditures made in Australia and other countries to other social security expenditures'-in those countries. In Australia the percentage is 24-6 per cent, in Great Britain 4-7 per cent and in New Zealand 23 per cent.
Therefore Canada's 27 [DOT] 7 per cent represents the fact that our family allowance program is larger in percentage of relation to social security expenditures than that of any other Of the countries with which- I think comparison is justified. That is significant. What my hon. friend has done tonight is to urge that, although Canada leads in that it is able to say that its family allowance payments represent a greater portion of social security expenditures than in these other countries, we should still increase that -expenditure and bring it, as he conceivably would if he carried his proposal to a logical conclusion, away out of proportion with existing social expenditures or other expenditures that he


and others propose from time to time in the house. He said that at the present time we were paying family allowances to some 2 million children. Well, he has underestimated the extent of this program. I am sure he meant to give the higher figure, which for the sake of accuracy is 4,513,000 children. In other words 4,513,000 children receive every month from the regional offices of the family allowance division moneys contributed by the taxpayers of Canada for the purposes envisaged in the Family Allowances Act. That is a tremendous figure. It represents 1,960,000 families, which is also a significant figure. The total monthly cost of this program to Canada is some $27 million a month. Hon. members have seen the departmental estimates for this year, and they will see that we are budgeting for a total of $332,150,000 for family allowances for this year.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to other members of this house, particularly the hon. gentleman in whose name this resolution stands, that this figure of $332,150,000 must be kept in mind in discussing a resolution such as that now offered to the house. In 1946 our total expenditure on family allowances was $240 million. When you realize that we are now spending $332 million on family allowances, altogether apart from the old age security payments which amount to well over $300 million, and which will increase because of our ageing population, while I would not say the hon. gentleman is not responsible, one has to clearly relate these figures to the capacity of this nation to meet these costs, particularly when we are committed to the extent of $2 billion by way of building up our defences. I think nothing would be more regrettable than to give our people the impression that there is no limit to what we can do in these matters. Nothing would be more unfortunate than to convey the impression that nothing is beyond the capacity of this nation which is now so heavily taxed; and I believe that on occasion no hon. gentleman is more vociferous in regard to the level of taxation this government has had to impose than the hon. gentleman who introduced this resolution. I can only say to him that the proposal he makes would only give increasing justification to those who sometimes deplore the extent of taxation.
My hon. friend says we should relate the cost of family allowances to the cost of living. I have had to do with the administration of these measures for six years now, which has given me an opportunity to see what other countries have done and what people who have spent a good bit of time studying these measures think about their relation to the

cost of living. If you want to damn a social security program, just relate it to that aspect of the problem. A social security program must be constant. It must be so arranged as to never encourage retrenchment. It must be so arranged as to be capable of improvement, not diminution. If you relate the cost of living at any one period to the social security benefit you will get the same result they got in France and Switzerland, where the total cost of many of these measures has gone far below the level when they were first introduced. The pretext given in every case I know of was that after the measures were introduced they were related to increases in the cost of living. When the cost of living went down the benefits were reduced, not only proportionately but often well below the original level. So on that ground alone I do not think the proposal of the hon. member is sound.
There is another consideration. My friend argues as though these family allowance payments or any of these social benefits were intended as complete grants to cover the total maintenance of a child or, in the case of the old age pension, an aged person.

I do not know of any country in the last three years that has adopted as important and as significant a social security program as Canada, at a time when it is calling upon its people to spend so much of its resources to arrest potential aggression in the world. On reflection, I know that my friend will leave this chamber tonight, go down the dignified pavement of parliament and will say: Well, you know, perhaps it was my-inexperience-my youthful impulsiveness-that led me to suggest that Canada was not leading the way at this time-

There have been abuses in the Family Allowances Act; there has been fraud. But the number of occasions on which we have had to authorize prosecutions is relatively insignificant in respect of a program that is costing us well over $300 million, but which for the purposes of administration is costing us less than $4 million. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
Prime Minister mentioned today that it has become urgent that we deal with legislation concerning the veterans because the delegation of the Legion will be in Ottawa next week and wish to see the legislation before they make their representations before the veterans affairs committee. Therefore tomorrow we will proceed witth the motion setting up the special committee on veterans affairs. Then we shall take up the resolution preceding the bills relating to veterans: first, the motion on legislation respecting the war veterans allowances; second, the motion on the Veterans Benefit Act, 1951; third, the motion on the Veterans Insurance Act; fourth, the motion on the Pension Act, and then we will revert to the debate on the budget.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
